title: How would you design a video streaming platform (e.g. YouTube/Netflix) — why uploads must be processed ASYNCHRONOUSLY (upload → queue → background worker → transcode with FFmpeg into multiple renditions → generate thumbnails → store → publish), adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH serving different qualities by bandwidth), serving segments from a CDN/edge rather than origin, object storage for the raw/encoded files, and view/analytics tracking?
shortTitle: How would you design a video streaming platform like YouTube or Netflix

s1_definition.profdef: A video streaming platform ingests uploaded video, processes it asynchronously through a pipeline (queue, background transcode with FFmpeg into multiple bitrate renditions, thumbnail generation, storage, publish), stores raw and encoded files in object storage, and serves playback via adaptive bitrate streaming using HLS or DASH where the player picks the quality that matches current bandwidth. Encoded segments are delivered from a CDN edge close to the viewer rather than the origin, and view and engagement events are tracked for analytics and recommendations.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India records training and KYC-verification videos for staff and customers like Rajesh and Priya. When someone uploads a raw recording, you cannot make them wait while it is converted into every quality, that could take minutes. So the upload is accepted instantly, dropped into an in-tray (queue), and workers in the back room convert it overnight into small, large, and medium versions and make thumbnail images. When Rajesh watches on a slow train connection, the player automatically plays the small version; on office WiFi it plays HD. And the video is served from a nearby copy (CDN edge) like a local branch instead of head office, so it loads fast everywhere.
s1_definition.oneliner: Accept uploads fast and transcode asynchronously into multiple renditions, store in object storage, stream adaptively with HLS/DASH so the player matches bandwidth, and serve segments from a CDN edge, not the origin.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A video streaming platform ingests uploaded video, processes it asynchronously through a pipeline (queue, background transcode with FFmpeg into multiple bitrate renditions, thumbnail generation, storage, publish), stores raw and encoded files in object storage, and serves playback via adaptive bitrate streaming using HLS or DASH where the player picks the quality that matches current bandwidth. Encoded segments are delivered from a CDN edge close to the viewer rather than the origin, and view and engagement events are tracked for analytics and recommendations.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India records training and KYC-verification videos for staff and customers like Rajesh and Priya. When someone uploads a raw recording, you cannot make them wait while it is converted into every quality, that could take minutes. So the upload is accepted instantly, dropped into an in-tray (queue), and workers in the back room convert it overnight into small, large, and medium versions and make thumbnail images. When Rajesh watches on a slow train connection, the player automatically plays the small version; on office WiFi it plays HD. And the video is served from a nearby copy (CDN edge) like a local branch instead of head office, so it loads fast everywhere.

**One line to remember:** Accept uploads fast and transcode asynchronously into multiple renditions, store in object storage, stream adaptively with HLS/DASH so the player matches bandwidth, and serve segments from a CDN edge, not the origin.

sections.s2_technical:
Why uploads must be processed asynchronously. Transcoding a video into multiple qualities with FFmpeg is CPU-heavy and slow, often many times the video's length. If you did it synchronously inside the upload request, the uploader would wait minutes and the request would time out, and a burst of uploads would exhaust your servers. So you decouple: the upload endpoint accepts the raw file (ideally via a presigned direct-to-storage upload), records metadata with status PROCESSING, and drops a job on a queue. Background workers consume jobs at their own pace, transcode, generate thumbnails, store the outputs, and flip the status to PUBLISHED. The uploader gets an instant response, and processing happens off the request path, scaling independently by adding workers.

The processing pipeline. A typical pipeline is: upload lands in object storage as the raw master; a message is published to a queue; a worker picks it up, validates the file, runs FFmpeg to produce several renditions (for example 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p) each segmented into short chunks, generates thumbnail images and a preview sprite, writes an HLS or DASH manifest describing the renditions, stores all outputs back in object storage, and publishes a VideoReady event that updates the catalog and makes the video available. Each stage is retryable, and a failed transcode goes to a dead letter queue for inspection.

Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH). A single fixed-quality file is wrong for the real world, where bandwidth varies by device and network. Adaptive bitrate streaming encodes the video at several bitrates, each split into small segments of a few seconds, and publishes a manifest listing them. The player downloads the manifest, then continuously measures its available bandwidth and picks the highest-quality segment it can download in time, switching up when the network improves and down when it degrades, segment by segment, with no rebuffering. HLS (Apple) and DASH (open standard) are the two dominant protocols; both work this way. This is why Netflix smoothly drops to lower quality on a weak connection instead of freezing.

Serving from a CDN edge, not the origin. Video is huge and heavily watched, so serving every segment from your origin storage would saturate it and give distant viewers high latency. Instead you put a CDN in front: the encoded segments are cached at edge locations around the world, and a viewer fetches segments from the nearest edge, which is fast and offloads the origin. The origin (object storage) is hit only on a cache miss. This is essential for scale and global low latency; the vast majority of video bytes are served from the edge.

Object storage for raw and encoded files. Videos are large binary blobs that do not belong in a relational database. You store the raw master upload and all encoded renditions, segments, manifests, and thumbnails in object storage such as S3 or GCS, which is cheap, durable, and effectively infinite. The database stores only metadata: video ID, title, owner, status, durations, and pointers to the storage keys. Lifecycle rules can move the raw master to cold storage after encoding since it is rarely needed again.

View and analytics tracking. You track playback events, start, pause, seek, quality switches, watch time, and completion, both to power recommendations and to monitor quality of experience (rebuffering rate, startup time, bitrate served). These events stream into an analytics pipeline. View counts need care at scale because naive per-view database increments do not keep up with millions of concurrent viewers, so you buffer and aggregate counts asynchronously rather than incrementing a row on every play.

The senior nuance is that this is two very different systems joined by object storage: a write-heavy asynchronous processing pipeline optimized for throughput, and a read-heavy global delivery system optimized for latency via CDN and adaptive streaming. You design each for its own goal and connect them through storage and events, never making the viewer wait on processing or the uploader wait on delivery.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India hosts video content: product explainer videos, training, and recorded video-KYC sessions. Customers like Rajesh (SAV2001) watch on varied devices and networks.

Problem 1 — uploads timed out while converting. The first version transcoded synchronously inside the upload request, so uploaders waited minutes and requests failed, and a few concurrent uploads overloaded the server. This is why we accept the upload instantly and transcode asynchronously via a queue and background workers.

Problem 2 — playback froze on slow connections. A single 1080p file buffered endlessly on Rajesh's train connection. This is why we transcode into multiple bitrates and serve adaptive bitrate streaming so the player drops to a lower quality smoothly.

Problem 3 — videos loaded slowly for distant viewers and hammered the origin. Serving every segment from central storage was slow and saturated. This is why we serve segments from a CDN edge close to the viewer.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of the processing pipeline and playback selection: an `UploadService` that accepts and enqueues, a `TranscodeWorker` that produces renditions and thumbnails (simulated FFmpeg), a `ManifestBuilder` for HLS, an object-storage stand-in, an `AdaptiveBitratePlayer` that selects a rendition by bandwidth, and a `ViewTracker`. It uploads a video, processes it asynchronously, and plays it back at different bandwidths.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/video-streaming-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.video.VideoDemo

# Run the service
java -jar target/video-streaming-service-1.0.0.jar

# Upload (returns instantly with status PROCESSING; bytes go direct to S3 via presigned URL)
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/videos \
  -d '{"ownerId":"SAV2001","title":"home_loan_explainer.mp4","sizeBytes":500000000}'

# FFmpeg command a worker runs (conceptual) to make a 480p HLS rendition
ffmpeg -i master.mp4 -vf scale=-2:480 -c:v h264 -b:v 1400k \
  -hls_time 6 -hls_segment_filename '480p/seg-%d.ts' 480p/manifest.m3u8
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh uploads a 500 MB product explainer video. He later watches on three different networks.

Step 1: The upload hits UploadService. The raw master is stored in the raw bucket (in production via a presigned direct-to-storage upload), metadata is recorded with status PROCESSING, a transcode job is enqueued, and the uploader gets an instant response. No transcoding happens on the request.

Step 2: The background TranscodeWorker polls the queue, picks up the job, and runs FFmpeg (simulated) to produce four renditions, 240p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, each segmented into short chunks, plus a thumbnail. It writes a master HLS manifest listing the renditions and stores everything in the encoded bucket.

Step 3: The worker flips the video status to PUBLISHED. Now it is available to viewers. All of this happened off the upload path, so the uploader never waited.

Step 4: Rajesh watches on office WiFi at about 8 Mbps. The adaptive player measures bandwidth and selects the highest rendition that fits, 1080p. On a train 3G at 1.2 Mbps it selects 480p. In a tunnel at 0.4 Mbps it drops to 240p. The player switches quality smoothly, segment by segment, so playback never freezes.

Step 5: Segments are fetched from the CDN edge URL, not the origin, so they load fast wherever Rajesh is and the origin storage is spared.

Step 6: The view tracker records PLAY, a quality switch, and COMPLETE as events. These stream to analytics; view counts are aggregated asynchronously rather than incremented per play.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Ingest + async processing (write path) ──
  Rajesh uploads 500MB
    │ presigned PUT → raw bucket   (instant accept, status PROCESSING)
    ▼
  job queue (Kafka video.transcode.jobs)
    │ consume
    ▼
  TranscodeWorker (FFmpeg, ×N workers)
    │ 240p / 480p / 720p / 1080p  (each segmented 6s)
    │ thumbnails + sprite
    │ write master HLS manifest
    ▼
  encoded bucket  →  status PUBLISHED  →  VideoReady event → catalog

  ── Playback (read path) ──
  Rajesh player downloads master manifest
    │ measure bandwidth
    ├─ 8 Mbps  → request 1080p segments
    ├─ 1.2 Mbps→ request 480p segments
    └─ 0.4 Mbps→ request 240p segments
            │ segment URL → CDN EDGE (cache hit)  ← not origin
            ▼
       smooth playback, switches quality per segment
            │
            ▼
       view events → analytics (async aggregation)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I design a video streaming platform as two very different systems joined by object storage: a write-heavy asynchronous processing pipeline optimized for throughput, and a read-heavy global delivery system optimized for latency. The single most important decision is that uploads are processed asynchronously. Transcoding a video into multiple qualities with FFmpeg is CPU-heavy and often takes many times the video's length, so if I did it inside the upload request the uploader would wait minutes and the request would time out, and a burst of uploads would melt my servers. Instead the upload endpoint accepts the raw file, ideally via a presigned direct-to-storage upload, records metadata with status processing, and drops a job on a queue, returning instantly. Background workers consume jobs at their own pace, transcode, generate thumbnails, store the outputs, and flip the status to published, scaling independently by adding workers. On my project at National Bank of India this fixed uploads that were timing out because we transcoded synchronously.

The processing pipeline runs the raw master through FFmpeg to produce several renditions, for example 240p, 480p, 720p, and 1080p, each split into short segments, generates thumbnails, writes an HLS or DASH manifest describing the renditions, and stores everything back in object storage, with each stage retryable and failures going to a dead letter queue. Playback then uses adaptive bitrate streaming, because a single fixed-quality file is wrong for the real world where bandwidth varies. The player downloads the manifest, continuously measures its available bandwidth, and picks the highest-quality segment it can download in time, switching up when the network improves and down when it degrades, segment by segment, which is why playback smoothly drops quality on a weak connection instead of freezing. This is how I fixed Rajesh's video freezing on a train.

Delivery is from a CDN edge, not the origin. Video is huge and heavily watched, so serving every segment from origin storage would saturate it and give distant viewers high latency. I put a CDN in front, so encoded segments are cached at edge locations worldwide and each viewer fetches from the nearest edge, hitting the origin only on a cache miss, which is essential for global low latency and offloading storage. The raw masters and all encoded renditions, segments, manifests, and thumbnails live in object storage like S3 because they are large binary blobs that do not belong in a database; the database holds only metadata and pointers to storage keys, and I can lifecycle the raw master to cold storage after encoding.

Finally I track playback events, start, pause, seek, quality switches, watch time, and completion, both to power recommendations and to monitor quality of experience like rebuffering and startup time. At scale I never increment a view count per play on a database row because that cannot keep up with millions of concurrent viewers, so I buffer and aggregate counts asynchronously. The overarching principle I state is that the uploader must never wait on processing and the viewer must never wait on processing either, so I decouple the two through object storage and events and design each side for its own goal.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I accept uploads instantly and transcode asynchronously through a queue and FFmpeg workers into multiple bitrate renditions stored in object storage, serve playback with adaptive bitrate HLS or DASH so the player matches the viewer's bandwidth segment by segment, deliver those segments from a CDN edge rather than the origin for global low latency, and track view and quality events through an async analytics pipeline.
